notes.front: What is the judicial branch?
notes.back: The branch that reviews laws; it is the Supreme Court and the other federal courts.
notes.explanation: It is the third branch, alongside the legislative and executive branches taught earlier.
notes.example: Like a school's own panel that checks that decisions follow the school's rules.

notes.front: What is the Supreme Court?
notes.back: The highest court in the United States; its decisions are final.
notes.explanation: It sits at the top of the judicial branch, above the lower federal courts taught next.
notes.example: Like a final court of appeal whose ruling cannot be appealed any further.

notes.front: What are the lower federal courts?
notes.back: The federal courts below the Supreme Court: courts of appeals (13 circuits) and district courts (94 districts).
notes.explanation: Most federal cases start and often end here, without ever reaching the Supreme Court.
notes.example: Most federal cases start in one of the 94 district courts.

notes.front: What is a justice?
notes.back: Another word for a judge on the Supreme Court; there are nine.
notes.explanation: On the US Supreme Court, the judges are called justices.
notes.example: Like a panel of nine senior reviewers, each with the title “justice” rather than “judge.”

notes.front: What is a lifetime appointment, for a federal judge?
notes.back: Federal judges can serve for the rest of their lives, or until they retire. (The Constitution says they "shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour".)
notes.explanation: It is a deliberate design choice, explained by judicial independence, taught next.
notes.source: Constitution Art. III, sec. 1; study guide p.29
notes.example: Like a role with no fixed term and no re-election, ending only by choice or serious misconduct.

notes.front: What is judicial independence?
notes.back: The Founders did not want judges to decide cases based on politics or elections; so judges are not elected.
notes.explanation: It is the reason federal judges get lifetime appointments instead of running for office.
notes.example: Like a referee who is hired for life so no team can vote them off the field.

notes.front: What is judicial review?
notes.back: Courts can decide whether a law follows the Constitution, but only when a legal case is brought before them.
notes.explanation: It is what “the judicial branch reviews laws” actually means in practice.
notes.example: Like an appeals panel that can strike down a policy, but only once someone actually challenges it.

notes.front: What is the Chief Justice of the United States?
notes.back: The justice who leads the Supreme Court.
notes.explanation: The office is fixed; only who currently holds it changes with a new appointment.
introduces: Chief Justice of the United States
notes.example: Like the presiding member of a nine-person panel, chosen to lead the others.

notes.front: What is one part of the judicial branch?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts naming the federal courts generally. Other accepted answers: Federal Courts.

notes.front: What does the judicial branch do?
notes.explanation: USCIS accepts several phrasings of the same reviewing role. Other accepted answers: Explains laws; Resolves disputes (disagreements) about the law; Decides if a law goes against the (U.S.) Constitution.

notes.front: What is the highest court in the United States?
notes.explanation: One of the 20 questions for 65/20 applicants. (65/20)

notes.front: How many seats are on the Supreme Court?
notes.explanation: There are nine justices.

notes.front: How many Supreme Court justices are usually needed to decide a case?
notes.explanation: Five of nine is a simple majority of the full Court.

notes.front: How long do Supreme Court justices serve?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts “lifetime appointment” and “(until) retirement.” Other accepted answers: Lifetime appointment; (Until) retirement.

notes.front: Supreme Court justices serve for life. Why?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts “to limit outside (political) influence,” the same idea in other words. Other accepted answers: To limit outside (political) influence.

notes.front: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
notes.explanation: Check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates before an interview, since this changes with appointments. Other accepted answers: John G. Roberts, Jr.; Roberts.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · verify at uscis.gov (as of USCIS's 09/18/2025 update)

notes.front: How many federal courts are there at each level: top, middle and bottom?
notes.back: 1 Supreme Court, 13 courts-of-appeals circuits, 94 district courts.
notes.explanation: This shows the federal court system as a pyramid, widest at the district-court base.

notes.front: Which branch of government is made up of the Supreme Court and the other federal courts?
notes.explanation: It is the branch that reviews laws, distinct from Congress and the President.

notes.front: Which court's decisions cannot be appealed to any higher court?
notes.explanation: It is the highest court, and its decisions are final.

notes.front: What is the title for one of the nine judges on the Supreme Court?
notes.explanation: On the US Supreme Court, the judges are called justices.

notes.front: A federal judge is not elected and has no fixed term. What is this arrangement called?
notes.explanation: It lasts until the judge dies, retires, or is removed for misconduct.

notes.front: Why are federal judges not elected?
notes.back: Judicial independence: so they decide cases on the law, not on politics or elections.
notes.explanation: It is the reasoning behind lifetime appointments.

notes.front: A court decides whether a law violates the Constitution, in a real case brought before it. What is this power called?
notes.explanation: Courts can only use this power once an actual case reaches them.

notes.front: Which Supreme Court justice leads the Court?
notes.back: The Chief Justice of the United States.
notes.explanation: The office, not the current name, is what this card tests.

notes.front: What is the difference between the Supreme Court and the lower federal courts?
notes.back: Supreme Court: the highest court, decisions final, 9 justices. Lower courts: 13 circuits of appeals plus 94 district courts, below it.
notes.explanation: Most federal cases are decided at the lower level and never reach the Supreme Court at all.
notes.contrast: Only the Supreme Court's decisions are final; a lower court's ruling can still be appealed upward.
